title: Protocol to Study Social Transmission of Stress in Group-Housed Mice Using Restraint Stress
author: Mink, Horvath, et al.
materials: C57BL/6 mice, aged 8–12 weeks, male and female
High variations in levels of corticosterone.
High variability in stress transmission group.
This study did not generate new unique reagents.

steps.title: Acclimate and habituate mice
steps.instruction: For 1–2 weeks, recruit littermate C57BL/6 mice (8–12 weeks old) and house four per cage with food and water ad libitum in a quiet room at controlled temperature and humidity, using a 12 h light‑dark cycle (lights on 07:00, off 19:00). Perform daily non‑aversive handling to habituate them to human interaction. Optionally collect baseline blood (submandibular or tail vein) 24 h before stress onset at the same circadian time as future sampling.

steps.title: Prepare restraint tubes and divider
steps.instruction: Construct restraint tubes from 50 mL conical tubes by drilling ~30–40 smooth‑edged holes for airflow and cutting a small lid section for the mouse tail. Fabricate an opaque acrylic cage divider whose height is just below the cage lid and width fits tightly to prevent movement; ensure it blocks visual contact but allows olfactory and auditory cues.

steps.title: Assign groups and mark animals
steps.instruction: Assign each cage to either a stress group or a control group. Within stress cages, uniquely mark each mouse and designate two as directly stressed (RS) and two as indirectly stressed (TS). Include unstressed control cages with the same marking scheme.

steps.title: Record baseline body weight
steps.instruction: Weigh each mouse before the first stress session and record the values for later normalization of organ weights.

steps.title: Set up cage configuration
steps.instruction: Transfer mice from the home cage to a separate cage. Insert the opaque acrylic divider to split the cage into two compartments. Place the two RS mice into prepared restraint tubes and position the tubes on one side of the divider. Place the two TS mice freely on the opposite side (they retain access to food and water). For control cages, place two mice on each side without restraint tubes.

steps.title: Apply restraint stress and interaction
steps.instruction: Restrict the RS mice for 4 hours while the divider remains in place. After 4 hours, release the RS mice from the tubes, remove the divider, and allow all four mice to interact freely for 20 hours. Repeat this procedure once for acute stress or daily for up to 10 days for chronic stress. Keep all additional manipulations (e.g., blood draws, injections) identical across stressed and control groups.

steps.title: Optional immunization on day 4
steps.instruction: On day 4 of a chronic stress schedule, give each mouse a sub‑cutaneous injection of 5 mg PLGA‑microparticles containing ovalbumin antigen and the adjuvant Riboxxim.

steps.title: Conduct behavioral testing
steps.instruction: Starting on day 7 of the stress regimen, perform one behavioral test per day: novel object recognition on day 7, open‑field test on day 8, and light/dark‑box test on day 9. Ensure testing occurs at consistent times and that mice are acclimated to the testing room for 1–2 hours beforehand.

steps.title: Collect samples post‑stress
steps.instruction: At a consistent circadian time (2–3 h after lights on), euthanize mice by CO₂ asphyxiation followed by cervical dislocation in a quiet room. Immediately perform cardiac puncture with a 1 mL syringe and 25–27 G needle to collect blood into EDTA‑ or heparin‑coated tubes.

substeps.instruction: Centrifuge blood at 2,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C; aliquot plasma and store at –80 °C.
Dissect and weigh both adrenal glands; optionally fix in 4 % formalin prepared in phosphate buffer (55 mM Na₂HPO₄, 12 mM NaH₂PO₄).
Remove thymus and spleen, weigh, and place in PBS on ice for downstream cell isolation or flow cytometry.
Optionally collect brain tissue for fixation or snap‑freezing.

steps.title: Process tissues for analysis
steps.instruction: Normalize adrenal and thymus weights to body weight. Prepare single‑cell suspensions from spleen or thymus for flow cytometry or in‑vitro stimulation (e.g., LPS 1 µg ml⁻¹ for 75 h). Perform ELISA or multiplex assays on plasma (corticosterone, IL‑6, TNF) and on culture supernatants as required.

The extent of these responses depends on the duration (acute vs. chronic) and sex of the animals. Effects after only one session of restraint stress (acute stress) and a 20 h social interaction period were very mild, but chronic stress transmission showed profound effects. This protocol can be combined with other interventions. We applied a vaccination model, however, alternative approaches such as genetic knockout systems or other drug interventions could likewise yield valuable data on the transmission of stress and its consequences. To confirm the induction of direct stress, we found that thymus atrophy was the most consistent and profound readout. In stress transmission mice, adrenal hypertrophy was the most consistent readout. Physiologically, both directly stressed and stress-transmission mice showed increased adrenal gland weight, indicating activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA)-axis (Figure 3).
